bridge: Builds on O01. Review addition, multiplication and division before the binary examples. No calculus is used.
teaching:
A positional number uses a base and place values. Decimal 47 is 4×10+7. Binary 1011 is 1×8+0×4+1×2+1=11. One bit has two possible values; eight bits form a byte with 256 possible patterns. A pattern needs an interpretation: the same byte can represent an integer, part of text or an instruction.

Hexadecimal groups four bits into one digit. The digits after 9 are A through F, representing 10 through 15. To convert a byte, split it into two groups of four bits. This makes hex a compact way to inspect data without claiming that those data are text.

Algebra describes relationships rather than particular values. If cost=quantity×price, dividing both sides by a nonzero quantity gives price=cost/quantity. Logarithms reverse exponentiation: log2(8)=3 because 2 cubed is 8. Security uses these ideas when reasoning about search spaces. Encoding is a representation rule, not secrecy: anyone who knows the rule can reverse it. Unicode code points and UTF-8 bytes are related but not interchangeable counts.

Encoding checkpoint: ASCII defines 128 codes using seven bits. Eight-bit storage and legacy extended encodings are separate choices. Unicode assigns code points; UTF-8 encodes those code points into bytes. For example, the emoji 😂 has code point U+1F602 (decimal 128514) and UTF-8 bytes F0 9F 98 82. Packing those four bytes into one integer is not its Unicode code-point number. A character, code point, byte and displayed glyph need not have a one-to-one relationship.
example:
Binary       Place values              Decimal  Hex
0010 1010    32 + 8 + 2                 42       2A
0100 0001    64 + 1                     65       41

2^4 = 16, so four bits have 16 patterns.
ASCII/UTF-8 letter A is byte 0x41.
UTF-8 letter é uses bytes C3 A9, not one byte.
explanation: For 2A, convert 2 to 0010 and A to 1010, then join. The value is 2×16+10=42. For A as text, 65 is its code point and one-byte UTF-8 value. For é, the code point is U+00E9 but UTF-8 uses two bytes. A length limit must say whether it counts characters, code points or bytes.
exercise: Convert 13 and 31 to eight-bit binary and two-digit hex. Solve 3×x=21. Calculate log2(32). Explain whether converting a message to hex protects confidentiality.
solution: 13=00001101=0D; 31=00011111=1F; x=7; log2(32)=5. Hex does not protect confidentiality because decoding needs no secret.
challenge: Convert binary 11110000 to decimal and hex. A field allows at most four UTF-8 bytes: do the strings AAAA and ééé fit? Explain every step without relying on a calculator result alone.
challenge_solution: 11110000=128+64+32+16=240=F0. AAAA uses four bytes and fits. ééé uses six UTF-8 bytes and does not. A character-count limit of four would make a different decision.
